name: Releases
one_liner: Done items from several iterations, delivered to users as a real product.
purpose: A Release is the result of the incremental process applied throughout several iterations: the team releases the solution as a viable product, or Minimum Viable Product, ready to be used by the stakeholders. By default the continuous exposure of Work Items plus demonstrated and validated iteration results already enable a solid Release, though specific requirements may demand extra validation against the Definition of Done. Releases introduce a timeboxed rhythm to the construction effort and give both the A-PCT and the stakeholders some predictability.
meta: An agreed Solution Increment delivered to client and users so they can start using it as a real product
All the Done Work Items from several prior iterations

The Release Plan artefact (§7.2.2.2, p. 78) — not a ceremony row

diagram.sec: 2. What makes a release more than an iteration end
items: It is delivered to client and users, who start using it as a real product
Default assurance comes from continuous exposure plus validated iteration results
Specific requirements may demand additional validation steps against the Definition of Done
Complex solutions may need extra preparation: training, fixing a critical bug, extra testing
Fixing a critical or major defect
Documenting aspects of the system (support and user documentation)
Additional functional, performance, load, system and integration testing
Training support personnel and end users
Updating the Development Plan and/or the Deployment Plan
One Transition Iteration may not be enough; the team may split into two sub-teams working in parallel
It is still an iteration: proper ceremonies, Iteration Planning with a Work Items List

diagram.sec: 4. The Release Plan — what it is for (p. 77)
items: Plan the release of usable versions of the solution
Provide a high-level plan with the main goals and major features to deliver
Give visibility of risks, issues, decisions, changes, constraints and assumptions of the development aspect
Assist in scheduling transition activities, aligned with the PM² Transition Plan
Assist in scheduling Business Implementation activities, aligned with the PM² Business Implementation Plan
Build it as early as possible — preferably at the start of the Planning phase
Provide different levels of detail: the AGB wants releases and objectives, the PrOw wants which items land where
Revisit it after each iteration, with the team's updated velocity
Feasibility = size of the WIL versus velocity; model optimistic and pessimistic velocity
Make assumptions clear and visible: velocity and the pre-defined iteration size
Have a Deployment Plan early; it can change both the WIL and the Release Plan
TeCo is Responsible for developing it; PM is Accountable for its alignment with the Charter
PrOw supplies the delivery strategy: milestone dates, release objectives, features and Work Items
ATeM and ArOw give viability, dependency and architecture input; BM is informed by the PrOw
A materially modified Release Plan may need review by the Project Steering Committee (p. 50)

fields.what: An agreed Solution Increment, delivered to client and users so they can start using it as a real product; contains all Done items from prior iterations.
fields.who: PrOw sets the strategy · A-PCT delivers
fields.pollux: Four releases: 29 Mar, 28 Jun, 27 Sep and 20 Dec 2029.

fields.what: The smallest viable version released so stakeholders can use it and the team can measure and learn from real usage.
fields.pollux: Release 1: exposure by member state, read-only — nothing else.

fields.what: A release includes only Done Work Items, judged against the team's Definition of Done, not merely against a story's acceptance criteria.
fields.pollux: WIL-127 met its criteria in the review but missed the DoD, so it missed the cut.

fields.what: The organisational strategy — marketing, operational, economic, legal, risk — that defines what, when and to whom the solution is delivered.
fields.who: Business owns it · PrOw carries it into the WIL
fields.pollux: Read-only first, then instrument depth, then external access, then self-service.

fields.what: Documents the high-level UX and development milestones: what will be released and when, based on what the PCT knows at that point in time.
fields.who: TeCo R · PM A · PrOw S
fields.pollux: Version 6 reissued after iteration 7's velocity drop.

fields.what: Different audiences need different depth: the AGB checks releases and objectives against strategy; the PrOw needs to know which Work Items land in which release.
fields.pollux: Medici sees four releases and their objectives; Curie sees the item-level split.

fields.what: Velocity and the pre-defined size of each iteration must be stated visibly as the plan's assumptions, because they drive everything else.
fields.pollux: "Velocity 34 points; iterations two weeks" printed on the plan's front page.

fields.what: Size of the Work Items List against team velocity; new facts change both continuously, so the plan is re-evaluated after each iteration.
fields.who: TeCo calculates · PrOw and BM adjust
fields.pollux: 202 points remaining ÷ 34 = six build iterations plus a transition iteration.

fields.what: An iteration devoted to making a release land: defect fixes, documentation, extra testing, user and support training, plan updates.
fields.pollux: Iteration 6 (19–30 Mar 2029) shipped Release 1 on Thu 29 Mar.

fields.what: A Transition Iteration has different activities but is not planned differently: proper ceremonies, Iteration Planning with a Work Items List, the same timebox.
fields.pollux: Iteration 6 still ran planning, stand-ups, a review and a retrospective.

fields.what: During a Transition Iteration the team may split into two sub-teams in parallel — one on release activities, one on features for the follow-on release.
fields.pollux: Babbage and Eiffel finished Release 1; Lamarr started Release 2 enablers.

fields.what: Depending on the solution, additional formalism and validation may be required before a release is accepted as compliant with the Definition of Done.
fields.pollux: DPC and LISO sign-off precedes any release opening access to national authorities.

fields.what: The strategy for deploying the software and its updates into production; planned early because it affects both the WIL and the Release Plan.
fields.pollux: Continuous delivery pipeline agreed with da Vinci's IT & Digital Division.

fields.what: For each planned release, transition activities and business implementation activities are documented and aligned with the PM² plans of the same name.
fields.who: BM and BIG plan the business side
fields.pollux: Four analysts retrained before Release 1 removes their quarter-end spreadsheets.

fields.what: The Release Plan makes visible the dependencies the information system has on other projects, systems or operations activities.
fields.pollux: Everything depends on the CASTOR lending platform, live since May 2028.

fields.what: Depending on the impact, a modified Release Plan may need to be reviewed by the Project Steering Committee before the change is agreed.
fields.pollux: Moving the scenario overlay out of Release 2 went to the PSC as a scope change.

fields.what: The outputs of the Release Planning steps — items added, updated, removed, and their relative estimates — must be incorporated into the Release Plan.
fields.who: PrOw R/A on the WIL · TeCo updates the plan
fields.pollux: Ran three times during iteration 7, on 04, 09 and 10 April.

fields.what: New velocity data generated at the Iteration Review is reflected in the Release Plan by the TeCo, then communicated to the PrOw.
fields.pollux: Lovelace reissued the plan after the 13 Apr review, before the retrospective's actions landed.

traps: A release is not an iteration end: it is delivered to users as a real product.
A Transition Iteration is still an iteration, with the full ceremony set.
The Release Plan is more than a calendar of dates — it carries the release strategy.
TeCo is Responsible for the Release Plan; the PrOw only supports it.
Only Done items ship; acceptance criteria alone do not make an item Done.
